name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python library for building and training deep learning models, created by François Chollet and now at version 3.0. It provides a high-level API that runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO, letting you write one codebase and switch backends. The one thing to know: Keras 3 is not just a TensorFlow wrapper anymore, it is a cross-framework language, so your choice of backend becomes a deployment detail rather than a rewrite.

sections.body: Keras is a deep learning library for Python, maintained by the Keras team and released under the Apache 2.0 licence. It first appeared in 2015 as a high-level interface for Theano and TensorFlow, and with Keras 3.0 it became a multi-backend framework that runs on JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only. In the AI stack it sits at the model-building layer: above the numerical backends that execute tensor operations, and below the application code that trains, evaluates, and serves models. The official site describes it as deep learning for humans, and the repository shows over 64,000 stars, indicating broad use.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the full model lifecycle: defining layers and models, training with fit(), evaluating with evaluate(), running inference with predict(), and saving or serializing models. It handles image classification, autoencoders, text generation with transformer decoders, and transfer learning from pre-trained weights. The built-in training loop works with NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. It is strongest when you want a readable, consistent API across experiments and production, and when you need to move between backends without rewriting model code. The official site does not claim it is the fastest option for every workload, and benchmarks show JAX typically leads on GPU, TPU, and CPU, though non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed for approachability. The Sequential API is a plain stack of layers, and the functional API adds flexibility for non-linear topology, shared layers, and multiple inputs or outputs. You need basic Python and a grasp of tensors and shapes, since layers must know their input shape to create weights. Some mathematics helps for understanding loss functions and optimizers, but the official guides start from loading MNIST and building a first model. The site offers guides on the Sequential model, the functional API, built-in training methods, and many examples, so a beginner can follow along without prior deep learning experience. The main prerequisite is comfort with Python and the willingness to read shape information in model summaries.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides cross-backend operations such as matmul, sum, stack, einsum, softmax, binary_crossentropy, and conv, so custom layers written with these ops work on all backends. KerasHub supplies pre-built components such as TokenAndPositionEmbedding and TransformerDecoder layers for text generation. The official site hosts guides, examples, and API documentation, and the project has a large community, with over 2.5 million developers reported as having chosen Keras. Integrations include tf.data, PyTorch DataLoader, NumPy, and Pandas.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, but the balance depends on your choices. The Sequential and functional APIs let you define a model in a few lines and train it with fit(), which is fast for prototyping. For production, Keras 3 lets you instantiate a model as a PyTorch Module, export it as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or use it as a stateless JAX function, and the distribution API supports model parallelism, data parallelism, and combinations, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch coming soon. The cost is that backend-specific optimizations may require leaving the pure Keras path, and the official site notes that benchmark results vary from model to model. If you need maximum control over memory and speed, you may need to drop into the backend directly.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: Keras is used by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine, according to the official Keras 3 page. It is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, especially after Keras 3 unified the API across backends. For someone choosing it for work, that means skills transfer across TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch environments, and existing tf.keras models that use built-in layers can run in JAX and PyTorch right away. The facts and the site do not give a breakdown of job listings or salary data, so claims about career outcomes beyond adoption should be treated as unsupported. The repository is actively maintained, with a last push in October 2026.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is typically used with Python and sits alongside JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch rather than replacing them. In a polyglot pattern, you might use Keras for model definition and training loops, then export to TensorFlow SavedModel for serving, or use JAX for high-performance training while keeping the same Keras code. The keras.ops namespace acts as a cross-framework language, so custom layers, models, and metrics written with it can be used in native JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch workflows. It also works with OpenVINO for inference-only deployments. The official site presents this as a way to write one codebase and run it on multiple backends, which reduces lock-in and lets teams choose the best runtime for each stage.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not the best choice when you need non-linear topology that the Sequential API cannot express, though the functional API covers most such cases. The distribution API is currently implemented only for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so multi-backend distributed training is not yet uniform. The official site does not state exact performance numbers for every model or backend, and it notes that benchmark results vary. It also does not detail memory management or low-level kernel control, which may matter for edge or embedded deployment. The site does not say how long the OpenVINO inference-only path will be maintained, or whether all KerasHub components work across every backend.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
